CWE-78.name: OS Command Injection
CWE-78.why: Attackers can manipulate OS commands to execute arbitrary code or access unauthorized server resources.
CWE-78.fix: Avoid executing system shell commands with user inputs. Use built-in programming language APIs, validate input strictly, or run commands in restricted sandboxes. See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.

CWE-89.name: SQL Injection
CWE-89.why: Attackers can manipulate your database queries to steal, delete, or modify data.
CWE-89.fix: Use parameterized queries (Prepared Statements) instead of string concatenation. Validate all user inputs. See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.

CWE-79.name: Cross-site Scripting
CWE-79.why: Attackers can inject malicious scripts that run in the victim's browser, stealing cookies or session tokens.
CWE-79.fix: Sanitize all user input and escape data before rendering it in HTML. Implement a Content Security Policy (CSP). See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.

CWE-352.name: CSRF
CWE-352.why: Attackers can trick users into performing actions (like changing a password) without their consent.
CWE-352.fix: Implement Anti-CSRF tokens in all state-changing forms (POST/PUT/DELETE). See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.

CWE-918.name: SSRF
CWE-918.why: Attackers can trick your server into making requests to internal services, cloud metadata endpoints, or other sensitive resources.
CWE-918.fix: Validate and sanitize all user-supplied URLs. Implement an allowlist of permitted domains and block internal IP ranges. See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.

CWE-284.name: Broken Access Control
CWE-284.why: Users can access resources or perform actions beyond their intended permissions, potentially viewing other users' data.
CWE-284.fix: Implement server-side authorization checks on every request. Deny access by default and use role-based access control. See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.

CWE-798.name: Hard-coded Credentials
CWE-798.why: Exposed hardcoded passwords, API keys, or secrets can be extracted by attackers to gain unauthorized access.
CWE-798.fix: Remove all hardcoded credentials. Retrieve configuration secrets at runtime from safe environment variables or key vaults. See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.

CWE-200.name: Information Exposure
CWE-200.why: Headers, debug logs, or database ports exposure can reveal your technology stack or sensitive data, helping attackers choose targeted exploits.
CWE-200.fix: Remove or mask version-revealing headers in your server config. Block access to public configuration directories. See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.

CWE-319.name: Cleartext Transmission
CWE-319.why: Insecure protocols like HTTP, Telnet, or FTP send data in plaintext, allowing network attackers to sniff credentials.
CWE-319.fix: Enforce HTTPS with TLS 1.2+, disable legacy protocols/ciphers, and replace FTP/Telnet with SFTP/SSH. See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.

CWE-310.name: Cryptographic Issues
CWE-310.why: Weak or missing encryption exposes sensitive data in transit. Attackers can intercept passwords, tokens, and personal information.
CWE-310.fix: Enforce HTTPS with TLS 1.2+. Disable legacy protocols (TLS 1.0/1.1) and weak ciphers (RC4, DES, 3DES). Use HSTS headers. See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.

CWE-693.name: Protection Mechanism Failure
CWE-693.why: Your server isn't instructing the browser on how to behave securely, leaving it open to Clickjacking or XSS.
CWE-693.fix: Configure your web server to send headers like 'X-Frame-Options', 'Strict-Transport-Security', and 'Content-Security-Policy'. See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.

CWE-770.name: Allocation without Limits
CWE-770.why: Without rate limiting, attackers can brute-force credentials, scrape data, or overwhelm your server with automated requests.
CWE-770.fix: Implement rate limiting at the application or reverse proxy level (e.g. Nginx limit_req, express-rate-limit). See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.

CWE-400.name: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption
CWE-400.why: The server may be vulnerable to denial-of-service attacks that can take the application offline for legitimate users.
CWE-400.fix: Deploy a WAF or DDoS protection service (e.g. Cloudflare). Implement connection and request rate limits. See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.

CWE-353.name: Missing Integrity Check
CWE-353.why: External scripts loaded without Subresource Integrity hashes can be tampered with if the CDN is compromised, injecting malicious code.
CWE-353.fix: Add integrity and crossorigin attributes to all external script/link tags. Generate hashes at srihash.org. See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.

CWE-538.name: Insertion of Sensitive Info into Externally-Accessible File
CWE-538.why: Files like .git/config, package.json, or CI configs are publicly accessible, potentially exposing source code and credentials.
CWE-538.fix: Block access to sensitive paths in your web server config. For Nginx: 'location ~* /\.git { deny all; }'. See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.

CWE-1104.name: Use of Unmaintained Third-Party Components
CWE-1104.why: Running outdated libraries with known CVEs gives attackers a ready-made exploit path into your application.
CWE-1104.fix: Upgrade the flagged library to the minimum safe version. Use automated dependency scanning (e.g. Dependabot). See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.

CWE-915.name: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes
CWE-915.why: Allowing clients to bind input parameters to internal object properties can let them overwrite restricted fields like isAdmin.
CWE-915.fix: Use Data Transfer Objects (DTOs) or explicit binding lists to specify exactly which properties can be modified by the client. See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.

CWE-862.name: Missing Authorization
CWE-862.why: Endpoints are accessible without validating if the user has permission, letting unauthenticated or lower-privileged users access restricted functions.
CWE-862.fix: Enforce backend authorization checks on all endpoints. Verify user privileges before processing requests. See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.

CWE-639.name: Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR)
CWE-639.why: User-supplied parameters (like IDs) are used directly to look up database records without verifying the requesting user owns that resource.
CWE-639.fix: Implement access control checks verifying that the authenticated user owns or is authorized to access the requested resource ID. See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.

CWE-285.name: Improper Authorization
CWE-285.why: Access control rules are applied incorrectly, such as relying on easily spoofable request headers (e.g. X-Forwarded-For or X-Original-URL) instead of verified session state.
CWE-285.fix: Perform all access control checks on the server side using cryptographically signed session tokens. Do not trust client-supplied HTTP headers for security decisions. See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.

CWE-863.name: Incorrect Authorization
CWE-863.why: Authorization logic can be bypassed by appending specific suffixes or abusing path parsing differences (path confusion) between reverse proxies and backends.
CWE-863.fix: Normalize and sanitize all request paths before performing authorization checks. Maintain uniform path mapping across proxies and backend application routing. See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.

CWE-269.name: Improper Privilege Management
CWE-269.why: The application trusts client-supplied query parameters or form fields (like role=admin) to determine user privileges, allowing privilege escalation.
CWE-269.fix: Determine user permissions solely from backend session state retrieved via a secure session identifier. Never trust client-supplied privilege parameters. See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.

CWE-306.name: Missing Authentication for Critical Function
CWE-306.why: Critical operations (like state-changing form submissions) are exposed without authentication, allowing anonymous callers to execute privileged actions.
CWE-306.fix: Require valid authentication tokens (e.g., sessions, JWTs) for all state-changing endpoints (POST/PUT/DELETE). See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.

CWE-942.name: Permissive CORS Policy with Credentials
CWE-942.why: The server reflects arbitrary Origin headers in its Access-Control-Allow-Origin response and enables credentials, allowing malicious sites to read sensitive user data.
CWE-942.fix: Never use wildcard or reflected origins when Access-Control-Allow-Credentials is set to true. Implement a strict allowlist of trusted origin domains. See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.

CWE-643.name: Improper Neutralization of Data Vulnerability in a Website ('XPath Injection')
CWE-643.why: Attackers can manipulate XML/XPath query structure to bypass authentication or extract sensitive XML database records.
CWE-643.fix: Use parameterized/variable-binding XPath APIs, validate input with strict allowlists, and return generic error messages rather than XML/XPath engine output. See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.

CWE-22.name: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')
CWE-22.why: Attackers can use special character sequences like '../' to escape the web root and read or write arbitrary files on the server's filesystem.
CWE-22.fix: Avoid passing user input directly to filesystem APIs. Use canonical paths verification, strict filename allowlisting, or store files using randomized IDs. See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.

CWE-548.name: Exposure of Information Through Directory Listing
CWE-548.why: Web servers configured to list directory contents allow attackers to discover hidden files, backups, and directory structures.
CWE-548.fix: Disable directory indexing (Options -Indexes in Apache, autoindex off in Nginx). Place default index.html files in all web-accessible folders. See https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/699.html for software development guidance.
